title: MemPalace
summary: MemPalace is a local-first AI memory system that stores everything you share verbatim, indexes it as a spatial palace of wings, rooms, and drawers with an AAAK closet index, and retrieves it with hybrid semantic + keyword search — no API key required for the core path. It never summarizes, never paraphrases, and never phones home, hitting ~96.6% R@5 on LongMemEval with zero LLM. This wiki maps the whole system for both humans and agents: ingestion, retrieval, interfaces, and the seven non-negotiable design principles that bind them together.
body: MemPalace is a local-first AI memory system: it stores every word you share verbatim, indexes it as a spatial memory palace of wings, rooms, and drawers, and retrieves it with hybrid semantic plus keyword search, all on your own machine with no API key required for the core path. It never summarizes, never paraphrases, and never phones home. The name comes from the ancient method of loci combined with Niklas Luhmann's Zettelkasten: wings group broad categories (people, projects, topics), rooms group by day or session, and drawers hold immutable verbatim chunks of about 800 characters. A separate index layer called closets stores compact AAAK pointer lines (entities, topics, key quotes) that an LLM can scan in one pass to know exactly which drawer to open. This wiki is a deep, cross-linked map written for both humans browsing the architecture and agents grepping for the exact module, symbol, and line. The core idea is to separate storage from retrieval: content is stored structured and lossless, but found unstructured. The AAAK index is a ranking signal, never a gate, so a weak or missing pointer can only help a search, never hide a drawer, which is why 100 percent recall is the design requirement rather than a side effect. Retrieval is hybrid vector plus BM25, reaching about 96.6 percent recall at 5 with zero LLM on LongMemEval, 98.4 percent held-out through the full hybrid pipeline, and at or above 99 percent with optional model-agnostic reranking. The codebase is roughly 30,000 lines of Python across about 48 modules at version 3.3.6, exposing 29 Model-Context-Protocol tools so agents can live inside the palace, with 14 UI locales and over 100 embedding languages. Seven design principles are non-negotiable: verbatim always, incremental only, entity-first, local-first with zero external API by default, performance budgets (hooks under 500 ms, injection under 100 ms), privacy by architecture, and background everything. Background hooks file memory off the chat window, saving roughly one US dollar per session by never re-transmitting diary blocks. Explore the major areas from here: ingestion (project mining, conversation mining, entities, AAAK dialect), retrieval (search, knowledge graph, storage backends), interfaces (CLI, MCP server, hooks), and the cross-cutting concerns of LLM integration, internationalization, security and privacy, maintenance, and benchmarks. Every page links to its neighbors, and the knowledge-graph diagram shows how the areas connect.

title: System Architecture
summary: MemPalace is a multi-layer AI memory system built on a pluggable storage backend (ChromaDB default) plus a SQLite knowledge graph. User data flows through miners into verbatim drawers, indexed by AAAK-compressed closets. The L0-L3 wake-up stack injects context on demand. Every component honors five non-negotiable principles: verbatim-always storage, append-only ingestion, local-first execution, background hooks, and privacy by architecture.
body: MemPalace is a multi-layer AI memory system with three concerns: ingestion (getting data in), retrieval (search and the wake-up stack), and the substrate that holds it (the pluggable storage backend and the SQLite knowledge graph). Ingestion runs through three miners - projects, conversations, and documents - which scan source files, split content into verbatim chunks called drawers, detect entities and wings/rooms, and route each drawer to palace storage. For every drawer the system builds AAAK-compressed closet pointers (topic plus entities plus quotes) so semantic search can locate relevant drawers quickly. All writes are append-only: a re-mine locks the source file, deletes prior stale drawers, then inserts fresh ones, so a crash mid-cycle leaves the palace untouched. Drawers live in the mempalace_drawers collection and closets in a separate mempalace_closets index. Search is hybrid: search_memories queries ChromaDB vector embeddings, gets candidate drawers, then re-ranks them with Okapi-BM25 scored over the candidate set's local corpus IDF. If vector search is disabled, it falls back to ChromaDB's SQLite FTS5 layer. Closets contribute only an optional boost weight - they are ranking signals, never gates - so weak or stale closets can never hide a strong BM25 match. Results are always verbatim drawer text with metadata: wing, room, source file, similarity. The wake-up stack has four layers. L0 is user identity read from ~/.mempalace/identity.txt. L1 is an auto-generated essential story scored by importance and recency, grouped by room, capped at 3200 chars. Together L0 plus L1 cost roughly 600 to 900 tokens and leave 95 percent of the context window free. L2 loads on-demand wing/room retrieval and L3 runs deep semantic search, each lazy and never blocking the chat. The storage backend follows an RFC 001 interface defined in backends/base.py with typed QueryResult and GetResult. ChromaBackend is the default reference implementation, wrapping ChromaDB's PersistentClient with HNSW bloat-guard tuning (batch_size and sync_threshold of 50000) to prevent link_lists.bin from ballooning on large mines. A separate SQLite knowledge graph stores subject-predicate-object triples with valid_from and valid_to dates for entity-first temporal reasoning; entity IDs are SHA256 of the name and triples are immutable. Concurrency is protected by mine_palace_lock, a per-palace, non-blocking, re-entrant lock that records the holder's PID and argv for diagnostics. Design principles are enforced by architecture: verbatim-always, incremental-only, entity-first, local-first embedding with optional BYOK external LLMs, sub-500ms hooks, and privacy by architecture. Background hooks sync new memory asynchronously with zero chat tokens.

title: The Palace Model
summary: MemPalace's spatial memory architecture: wings contain rooms, which hold immutable verbatim drawers; closets index them; hallways and tunnels connect entities and wings; dynamics make connections fade or strengthen by use.
body: The Palace Model is MemPalace's spatial memory architecture, mapping the method of loci and the Zettelkasten onto concrete data structures. A palace is organized as a tree. Wings are named broad categories derived from directory names, normalized to lowercase with underscores replacing hyphens and spaces. Rooms are time- or topic-based groupings within a wing, detected from file paths, filenames, or keywords during mining. Drawers are immutable chunks of verbatim source text of about 800 characters, identified by a deterministic SHA256 hash of the source file path plus chunk index, wrapped as drawer_WING_ROOM_hexsuffix. Each drawer stores original content plus metadata: wing, room, source file, chunk index, filed_at ingestion time, a detected hall keyword, entities (capitalized words appearing two or more times), and optionally content_date, line_start, and line_end for precise source location under Tier 6a. Closets are the searchable index layer in the mempalace_closets collection. The builder reads the first 5,000 characters of a drawer and emits atomic pointer lines for topics, double-quoted spans, and entity pairs, then packs them greedily into closet documents up to 1,500 characters without splitting a line. Pointer lines come in legacy three-segment form and Tier 6a four-segment form with an optional date and line span, falling back when fields are missing so old and new pointers coexist. Hallways are within-wing connectors materializing entity-pair co-occurrence: any pair appearing together in two or more drawers gets a hallway record tracking the pair, count, and rooms, persisted in hallways.json with symmetric IDs from the sorted entity pair. Tunnels are cross-wing links in three flavors: explicit user-created links, auto-generated topic tunnels using synthetic topic: room identifiers, and auto-generated entity tunnels using entity: identifiers, all stored in tunnels.json and deduplicated by canonical sorted-endpoint ID. Dynamics give both hallways and tunnels a living-connection layer with four fields: strength as a Hebbian weight between 0.05 and 5.0, stability as decay resistance, last_activated, and access_count. Hebbian potentiation grows strength on co-access; Ebbinghaus exponential decay fades it over time floored at 0.05; and the Cepeda spacing effect grows stability only when reinforcement is spaced more than an hour apart. Critically, dynamics fields are preserved across re-mines so accumulated salience never resets. On search, queries hit closets first, parse out drawer IDs, fetch those drawers, and rank by distance, falling back to direct drawer search. The palace_graph module builds a cached in-memory graph from drawer metadata with a 60-second TTL invalidated on writes.

title: Glossary
summary: An alphabetized reference for the entire MemPalace vocabulary, with each of the 100+ terms ending in a pointer to the page that covers it in depth. Covers the spatial model, the retrieval stack, the ingestion machinery, and the cross-cutting design principles.
body: The Glossary is a single alphabetized reference covering more than one hundred MemPalace terms, each ending with a pointer to the page that explains it fully. It draws every distinct domain term from the per-page concept sidecars and merges duplicate definitions, keeping the clearest one. The spatial-model vocabulary is the backbone: a wing is a broad person or project category, a room is a time or topic grouping inside it, and a drawer is an immutable ~800-char chunk of verbatim source text identified by a deterministic SHA-256 ID. Closets are the compact index records that hold topic, entity, and quote pointer lines back to drawers, packed greedily to 1500 chars. Hallways connect entity pairs within a wing, tunnels link rooms across wings, and a diary is a dated transcript whose content_date enables temporal grouping. A living Dynamics layer (Hebbian strength, Ebbinghaus decay, Cepeda spacing) ranks those connections by real use. The retrieval stack defines hybrid search as a two-stage process: semantic top-50 candidates from the HNSW vector index, then a convex re-score of 0.6 times vector similarity plus 0.4 times normalized Okapi-BM25, with closet boost and temporal proximity. Cosine distance lives in the [0,2] range, effective distance is the value after boost, and BM25-only over SQLite FTS5 is the graceful fallback when the vector index is corrupt. The L0-L3 wake-up stack injects context on demand: L0 identity, L1 essential story (~600-900 tokens together), L2 wing/room retrieval, and L3 deep semantic search. Ingestion terms cover the AAAK dialect (a pipe-separated symbolic index an LLM scans in one pass), idempotent and incremental ingest, drawer sweeps, NORMALIZE_VERSION, the COCA content-word filter, the two-signal-category rule, corpus-origin detection, and virtual line numbering. The knowledge-graph terms include RDF-style triples, validity windows, as_of temporal queries, invalidation, provenance fields, and timelines. Cross-cutting principles are defined too: local-first execution, BYOK external providers that are never silent, privacy by architecture, never-silent-fallback, input-validation sanitizers, symlink defense, and MCP stdio protection. Storage abstractions such as BaseBackend, BaseCollection, PalaceRef, and the typed QueryResult and GetResult dataclasses round out the list, along with i18n concepts like BCP 47 tags, combining marks, script-aware boundaries, and Matryoshka representation learning. Each entry links to architecture, palace-model, search, entities, knowledge-graph, backends, hooks, and the other detailed pages.

title: Project Mining
summary: Project mining scans a directory tree, detects file formats, chunks text into drawers with virtual line numbering, and stores them idempotently using deterministic SHA-256 drawer IDs. Re-mining never duplicates; it upserts to the same rows.
body: Project mining turns a directory of source files into verbatim, searchable drawers stored in the palace. The pipeline starts with scan_project, which walks the filesystem recursively, respects .gitignore rules, skips cache directories like .git, __pycache__, .venv and node_modules, ignores symlinks, filters by readable extension, and drops files larger than 500 MB. For each surviving file, process_file reads its bytes as utf-8 with errors replaced, then routes the file to a room via detect_room using a four-tier priority: folder path, filename, keyword scoring in the first 2000 characters, and a general fallback. Content is split by chunk_text into 800-character chunks with 128-character overlap, breaking at paragraph or line boundaries when possible. Each chunk gets 1-indexed line ranges computed with str.count to avoid quadratic slicing on huge files. Before writing, file_already_mined checks whether drawers already exist, whether the normalize version is stale, and whether the file mtime differs from the stored source_mtime within a 0.001-second tolerance. When a re-mine is needed it purges stale drawers and upserts fresh ones in batches of 1000. Drawer IDs are deterministic SHA-256 hashes of source_file plus chunk_index, so re-runs and parallel mines converge on the same rows without duplicates. Metadata enrichment via _build_drawer_metadata extracts a content_date through a five-tier hierarchy of filename, YAML frontmatter, content body, and mtime; tags entities from known_entities.json plus repeated capitalized words filtered by a COCA stoplist; and detects a hall by keyword scoring. After chunks are upserted, build_closet_lines produces compact pointer lines of the form topic|entities|date:Lstart-Lend|drawer_ids, with the Tier 6a date and line segment included only when metadata is present, and legacy three-segment pointers otherwise. Post-mine graph construction links wings sharing topics, builds within-wing entity hallways, and materializes cross-wing tunnels, all fault-tolerantly. The design is incremental and append-only: drawers are stored verbatim, line numbering is applied at read time, and a crash mid-batch leaves completed batches intact. Binary office formats are handled by a separate format_miner module using MarkItDown, with RTF routed to striprtf because MarkItDown cannot convert it.

title: Conversation Mining
summary: MemPalace converts diverse chat export formats (Claude Code JSONL, ChatGPT, Gemini CLI, OpenAI Codex, Slack, Claude.ai JSON) into a normalized >-prefixed transcript via the --mode convos pipeline. The primary miner chunks by exchange pair or extracts memory types, the sweeper catches per-message outliers, and diary ingest files daily summaries with incremental change detection.
body: Conversation mining is a multi-path ingestion pipeline that turns AI chat transcripts into searchable drawers in the MemPalace. Files enter through scan_convos, where the normalize function auto-detects the export format from extension and content shape, then dispatches to format-specific parsers for Claude Code JSONL, ChatGPT mapping trees, Gemini CLI, OpenAI Codex, Slack JSON exports, and Claude.ai JSON. Each parser extracts (role, text) message pairs and converts them to a canonical greater-than-prefixed transcript. The strip_noise function removes Claude Code system tags, hook output, and UI chrome using patterns anchored to line boundaries that refuse to cross blank lines, preventing a stray tag in one message from eating content in adjacent messages. Tool results are truncated per message: Bash output uses head and tail windows, Grep and Glob cap at twenty matches, and Read, Edit, and Write results are omitted entirely. After normalization, chunk_exchanges groups each user turn with the AI response that follows as one drawer, preserving question and answer semantics rather than splitting at arbitrary character boundaries. If fewer than three quote markers are found it falls back to paragraph then line-group chunking. General extract mode instead pulls five memory types: decisions, preferences, milestones, problems, and emotional. Each chunk gets a room via keyword scoring and a hall via cached config keywords, and a deterministic drawer ID derived from source file, extract mode, and chunk index. When NORMALIZE_VERSION bumps, prefetch_mined_set scans the palace once to collect already-mined files, turning O(n) per-file queries into one paginated pass that saves about an hour on large palaces. Pre-v2 drawers are purged before fresh chunks upsert so schema versions never mix. A secondary sweeper processes Claude Code JSONL message by message, using a timestamp cursor and deterministic IDs keyed by session and message uuid for idempotent, resume-safe ingestion; it uses strictly-less-than cursor comparison so siblings sharing a timestamp are not lost after a crash. Diary ingest splits daily summary files on double-hash headers, hashes content with SHA-256 to detect changes, and packs entries into closets in the AAAK dialect without splitting mid-topic. RFC 002 source adapters declare transformations and register via setuptools entry points, invoked through a PalaceContext facade.

title: Entity System
summary: MemPalace's entity system detects and classifies proper nouns (people, projects, topics) from content using a two-pass signal-based approach: i18n-aware regex extraction with COCA content-word filtering, then contextual signal scoring. A persistent EntityRegistry seeds from onboarding, learns high-confidence candidates, and optionally researches unknowns via Wikipedia. Corpus-origin detection separates AI agent personas from real people before classification.
body: The MemPalace entity system detects and classifies the people, projects, and topics named in your text. Detection runs in two passes. Pass one, extract_candidates, applies language-aware regex patterns loaded from i18n entity sections, matching single-word candidates against per-script character classes (ASCII, Latin with diacritics, Cyrillic, Devanagari) and multi-word candidates through separate phrase patterns. Locale-specific stopwords remove articles and particles. The COCA content-word filter then removes about 600 common English words such as Code, Line, Phase, and Note that appear capitalized but are never entities. Crucially the multi-word path bypasses the COCA filter so compounds like Claude Code survive even though bare Code is suppressed. Only names appearing at least three times advance to scoring. Pass two, score_entity, scores each candidate across six signal types: dialogue markers weighted three times, person verbs weighted two times, pronoun proximity within three lines weighted two times, direct address weighted four times, versioned or hyphenated forms as a project signal weighted three times, and code-file references weighted three times. A guard requires bare colon-prefix dialogue patterns to occur at least twice so metadata lines like Created: 2026-04-21 do not register as speaker tags. Classification by classify_entity enforces the two-signal-category rule: a person needs signals from two distinct categories with a person score of at least five, or a strong pronoun-only signal where pronoun hits are at least five and the pronoun-to-frequency ratio is at least 0.2. This prevents syntactic artifacts like Click, click, click from being read as a person. Before detection, corpus-origin detection determines the platform and any agent-persona names. Tier one is a heuristic counting unambiguous AI brand terms and ambiguous terms under a co-occurrence rule that prevents French novels and astrology forums from false-positiving as AI dialogue. Tier two optionally uses an LLM to extract agent-persona names, which are reclassified out of the people bucket so AI instances never populate family or relationship drawers. The persistent EntityRegistry at ~/.mempalace/entity_registry.json stores three tiers: onboarding, learned, and wiki, with Wikipedia research local-only by default unless network access is explicitly granted, saved via atomic write-then-rename. Detected entities feed closet pointer lines during mining and entity-pair co-occurrence graphs in hallways, keying the entire wing-navigation model and enabling entity-centric search.

title: AAAK Dialect & Closets
summary: AAAK is a lossy symbolic summarization format that turns verbatim drawer content into compact closet pointer lines an LLM can scan in one pass. Closets index drawers; retrieval scans closets to boost matching drawers while always returning verbatim content, preserving 100% recall.
body: AAAK Dialect and Closets are the index layer of the MemPalace ingestion pipeline. Drawers hold verbatim 800-character chunks of content; closets are a thin searchable index on top of them, modeled on the Zettelkasten method where small cross-referenced index cards point to larger source materials. AAAK is the dialect that turns a drawer into a closet line: a single compact pipe-separated line (typically 40 to 150 bytes) holding extracted entities, topics, key quotes, emotion codes, and importance flags. AAAK is explicitly NOT lossless compression; the original text cannot be reconstructed from AAAK output. Instead it is a structured summary layer that points back to the original verbatim drawers via the arrow syntax, so 100 percent recall is preserved because nothing is lost, only indexed. During mining, build_closet_lines in palace.py extracts topics via an action-verb regex (built, fixed, wrote, added, pushed, deployed), entities as proper nouns appearing two or more times in a 5000-character extraction window, and quotes as double-quoted strings, filtering entities against a hardcoded stoplist and the COCA corpus. Lines are packed greedily into closets capped at 1500 characters, never splitting a line across closets, rolling to numbered closets when full. Dialect.compress turns any plain text into AAAK by detecting emotional tone and importance flags through keyword matching, ranking topics with TF-IDF plus a proper-noun boost, and scoring a key sentence. Emotion detection uses 30 plus hardcoded keyword mappings with no machine learning and no API calls, making it instant, deterministic, and zero-token. During search the searcher queries closets and drawers in parallel; closets are a ranking signal, never a gate. A drawer from a source whose closet matched receives an ordinal rank-based boost from CLOSET_RANK_BOOSTS of 0.40, 0.25, 0.15, 0.08, 0.04, applied only when closet distance is at most 1.5, because closet distances cluster in the 1.2 to 1.5 range on narrative content and ordinal position is the more reliable signal. Non-Latin scripts are supported through i18n script-aware boundaries: _script_boundary replaces Python's word boundary with a lookaround so Devanagari, Arabic, Hebrew, and Thai combining marks are treated as inside-word, preventing names from being truncated. LLM-assisted closet regeneration via closet_llm is completely optional; regex closets always work offline, and LLMConfig rejects non-HTTP endpoint schemes at init to prevent exfiltration. Layer 1 generation pulls high-weight and flagged moments into a wake-up summary an LLM can scan in one shot.

title: Search & Retrieval
summary: MemPalace fuses vector semantic search with keyword-based BM25 scoring and optional closet-boosting to approach perfect retrieval, reaching 96.6% R@5 with zero LLM and 98.4% on held-out data through the full hybrid pipeline.
body: MemPalace Search and Retrieval combines vector semantic search with keyword-based BM25 scoring and optional closet-boosting for near-perfect recall. The baseline reaches 96.6% R@5 on LongMemEval with zero LLM, the full hybrid pipeline hits 98.4% R@5 on held-out data, and optional Haiku reranking reaches 100%. The architecture ensures weak semantic matches can be rescued by strong keyword overlap or temporal and preference signals, eliminating the pure-vector cold-retrieval problem. Search runs as a layered pipeline. Vector candidate selection is the floor that always runs: every search begins with drawer-direct vector retrieval through ChromaDB's HNSW index, over-sampling n_results times three candidates before ranking. The query is embedded with the configured model, either minilm or embeddinggemma, compared against all drawer embeddings in the requested wing or room, and candidates are collected with raw cosine distances. Subsequent ranking steps can only reorder, never suppress. If a closets collection exists, the system queries it separately and builds a per-source boost table. The top closet for a source yields a 0.40 distance reduction, the second 0.25, down to 0.04 for rank five, applied only when the closet distance is at or below 1.5. Boosts use the closet's ordinal rank, not absolute distance, because narrative content clusters closet distances in the 1.2 to 1.5 range regardless of match quality. After candidate gathering, hybrid rank applies Okapi-BM25 to the candidate-set text. IDF is computed locally over the candidates themselves, corpus-relative not global, so discriminativeness reflects each term's prevalence within the rerank pool. Vector similarity is computed as max of zero and one minus distance into the zero-to-one range, using absolute distance so adding or removing a candidate cannot reshuffle the others. BM25 is min-max normalized within the pool. The final score is 0.6 times vector similarity plus 0.4 times normalized BM25. Effective distance is clamped to the zero-to-two cosine range to keep boosts monotonic. Before embedding, the query sanitizer strips system-prompt contamination using a four-step fallback: passthrough if under 200 characters, question extraction, tail-sentence extraction, then tail truncation, recovering recall from 1 percent to 70 to 80 percent in worst-case contamination scenarios. Union candidate strategy also pulls BM25-only candidates from SQLite FTS5 and merges them with chunk-precise dedup keyed on source file and chunk index. Drawer-grep enrichment expands closet hits that span multiple chunks. When HNSW is unavailable, a BM25-only SQLite fallback reads from chroma.sqlite3 via the FTS5 trigram index so search never crashes. Closets are a ranking signal, never a filter gate, honoring the verbatim-always principle that nothing is thrown away. Key symbols include search_memories, _hybrid_rank, _bm25_scores, sanitize_query, get_embedding_function, and the CLOSET_RANK_BOOSTS constant.

title: Temporal Knowledge Graph
summary: The Temporal Knowledge Graph stores structured facts as subject-predicate-object triples with optional valid_from/valid_to timestamps, enabling queries at specific points in time. Built on local SQLite with thread-safe WAL mode and no external dependencies, it complements vector search with deterministic relationship queries and serves as ground truth for fact-checking and entity disambiguation.
body: The MemPalace Temporal Knowledge Graph stores structured facts as subject-predicate-object triples (RDF style) with optional valid_from and valid_to timestamps, so callers can ask what was true at a specific instant. It is built on a single local SQLite database at ~/.mempalace/knowledge_graph.sqlite3 with Write-Ahead Logging for durability and concurrent reads, zero external dependencies, and no subscriptions. A threading lock guards every database operation; the connection uses check_same_thread False and a 10-second busy timeout. Each KnowledgeGraph instance is a singleton per palace path, cached in mcp_server._kg_by_path so there is a single writer and consistent reads. The schema has two tables: entities (id, name, type, properties JSON) and triples (subject, predicate, object, valid_from, valid_to, confidence, provenance fields) with indexes on subject, object, predicate, and the temporal columns. Temporal values accept both legacy date-only YYYY-MM-DD and canonical UTC YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ formats. Date-only values are normalized at query time via SQL CASE expressions: valid_from becomes T00:00:00Z and valid_to becomes T23:59:59Z, so a date is treated as a full 24-hour window and as_of queries with canonical UTC datetimes still match older facts. The _temporal_filter_sql function assembles the WHERE clause. add_triple auto-creates missing entity nodes, normalizes the predicate to lowercase with underscores, generates a unique triple_id from a hash of valid_from and the current timestamp, validates that valid_to is not before valid_from (raising ValueError on an inverted interval, which would otherwise be invisible to every query), and deduplicates identical open triples. query_entity reads facts in three directions: outgoing, incoming, or both, joining entity names. invalidate closes a fact by setting valid_to and is idempotent, finding only triples with valid_to IS NULL. The KG does not enforce referential integrity at write time; the foreign key on subject is a soft constraint because entities are auto-created. timeline returns up to 100 facts chronologically. The KG is ground truth for fact_checker.py contradiction and name-confusion detection and for entity_registry.py disambiguation, and is ingested by project and conversation miners through adapters carrying RFC 002 section 5.5 provenance. SQLite was chosen over Neo4j for a local-first, zero external API design.

title: Storage Backends
summary: MemPalace abstracts storage behind a minimal typed interface (BaseCollection, BaseBackend) so retrieval implementations swap without touching mining, search, or repair code. ChromaDB is the reference backend; others register via setuptools entry points. Typed results, HNSW health checks, and per-palace write locks make the layer robust.
body: MemPalace's storage layer is roughly 2535 lines across four modules: the contract in base.py, the ChromaDB implementation in chroma.py, the registry resolver in registry.py, and the migration recovery path in migrate.py. Callers such as miners, searchers, and repair tools only touch the abstract contract. BaseCollection defines six required kwargs-only methods (add, upsert, query, get, delete, count) plus optional update, close, and health hooks. BaseBackend is the per-palace factory owning get_collection, close_palace, close, health, and an optional detect hook; it is lightweight on construction with connection deferred to get_collection, and thread-safe for concurrent multi-palace access. PalaceRef is a value object with id, local_path, and namespace that replaces legacy path-string arguments. Chroma returns raw dicts; MemPalace wraps them in QueryResult and GetResult frozen dataclasses that preserve the outer query dimension even when hits are empty and support attribute access as the primary API, with a dict-compatibility shim retained as a migration bridge. Fields not requested via include are empty lists, except embeddings which stays None. ChromaBackend runs three cold-start safety passes before opening a palace: fixing the seq_id BLOB migration bug, quarantining unpickleable index_metadata.pickle to avoid Rust SIGSEGV, and quarantining stale HNSW segments with mtime drift beyond 300 seconds or link/data payload ratios over 10x. These run once per palace per process gated by a quarantined paths set. The hnsw_capacity_status probe compares the sqlite embedding count against the HNSW element count via low-level queries, flagging real divergence so search can fall back to BM25, catching the failure mode where max_elements froze while sqlite kept growing. The registry discovers backends via importlib.metadata entry points under mempalace.backends; get_backend returns a cached singleton and resolve_backend_for_palace follows an explicit-config-env-detect-default priority. Per-palace write locking wraps upsert, add, and delete in mine_palace_lock so MCP tool writes and mine CLI invocations cannot corrupt link_lists.bin; the lock is reentrant per thread to avoid self-deadlock. The HNSW bloat guard sets batch_size and sync_threshold to 50000 at collection creation to prevent sparse-file bloat. Pickle reads are protected by a byte-sniff health check and a whitelist-only unpickler. Migration verifies a real write roundtrip to catch silent-noop collections, and falls back to raw SQLite extraction for version-mismatched palaces. Collections must be created with hnsw:space=cosine; legacy palaces missing this silently use L2 distance and produce nonsensical relevance scores.

title: CLI & Onboarding
summary: MemPalace's CLI dispatches 14 primary commands and onboarding guides first-time users through mode, entity, and embedding-model choices before mining begins.
body: MemPalace's CLI in cli.py dispatches fourteen primary commands including init, mine, search, wake-up, status, repair, and maintenance tooling, while onboarding.py guides first-time users through interactive setup. The init command, cmd_init at cli.py line 230, orchestrates a four-pass setup. Pass 0, run by _run_pass_zero at line 106, detects whether a corpus is AI-dialogue versus code or docs using a two-tier system. Tier 1 always runs cheap regex heuristics with no API call via detect_origin_heuristic. Tier 2 optionally runs an LLM refinement via detect_origin_llm to extract platform, user name, and agent persona names, but it critically does not override the heuristic's likely_ai_dialogue and confidence fields. This protects against weak local models like Ollama gemma4:e4b flipping a confident regex answer, a decision settled in the PR 1211 review. The result is persisted to origin.json with evidence trails prefixed Tier-1 heuristic or Tier-2 LLM. Pass 1 calls discover_entities to scan manifests, git authors, and prose. Pass 2 calls detect_rooms_local to infer room structure from folders. Pass 3 protects per-project files from accidental git commits. Init is idempotent because _gather_origin_samples skips mempalace's own artifacts, entities.json and mempalace.yaml, so re-runs do not drift in classification density. Pass 0 samples are capped at 30 files, 100 KB per file, and 5 MB total, with Tier 2 LLM samples trimmed to 2 KB each and 20 max. The mine dispatcher cmd_mine at line 489 routes to three miners based on the mode flag: projects for code and docs, convos for Claude, ChatGPT, and Slack transcripts with optional auto-classification, and extract for PDF, DOCX, XLSX, and PPTX office documents. Wake-up, cmd_wakeup at line 712, instantiates a MemoryStack and concatenates Layer 0 identity with Layer 1, the top 15 importance-scored drawers, totaling roughly 600 to 900 tokens, with hard truncation at MAX_CHARS 3200. Onboarding, run_onboarding at onboarding.py line 390, prompts for mode, embedding model, people, and projects, defaulting to the multilingual embeddinggemma model because English-only MiniLM collapses cross-lingual cosine similarity to about 0.35. It generates AAAK bootstrap and critical-facts files. The instructions CLI exposes five markdown instruction files consumed by the skill harness. Every LLM step is best-effort and never blocks setup, preserving the offline, no-API-key-required promise.

title: MCP Server & Tools
summary: The MemPalace MCP server exposes around 29 JSON-RPC tools that let Claude Code and Claude Desktop read and write the palace, mutate the temporal knowledge graph, manage cross-wing tunnels, and append agent diaries.
body: The MemPalace MCP server (mcp_server.py, 2,869 lines) exposes the entire palace read, write, and knowledge-graph interface as roughly 29 JSON-RPC 2.0 tools for Claude Code and Claude Desktop, communicating over stdio without network round-trips. main() restores the real stdout, configures UTF-8 on Windows, starts the idle watchdog, then loops reading JSON-RPC requests from stdin. handle_request() routes initialize, ping, tools/list, and tools/call methods, validates parameter types against each tool's input schema, whitelists unknown arguments, and writes responses to stdout. A central design concern is stdio protection: before any imports, the module saves the real stdout fd via os.dup, redirects fd 1 to fd 2 (stderr), and sets sys.stdout to sys.stderr, preventing transitive dependencies like chromadb and onnxruntime from writing C-level banners that would corrupt the JSON-RPC stream. _restore_stdout undoes both the fd and Python-level redirects in main. Cache management uses inode plus mtime staleness detection on chroma.sqlite3: _get_client compares current st_ino and st_mtime against cached values, and an inode change (full rebuild) or mtime change (external write greater than ten milliseconds) triggers a ChromaDB client rebuild. Before opening the client, _refresh_vector_disabled_flag probes HNSW capacity via a pure sqlite and pickle read, never touching chromadb, so the issue 1222 divergence flag is set before segment load to avoid segfaults. Knowledge graph operations run through _call_kg, which captures the canonical KG path once via realpath and normcase and retries once on sqlite3.ProgrammingError when a handle is closed mid-operation during reconnect. Write tools log to a write-ahead log at the home mempalace wal directory before mutating, with content, query, and entry fields redacted via a frozenset of keys. tool_add_drawer detects idempotency by probing drawer_id and the last chunk id, and chunks oversized content into a single batched all-or-nothing upsert. Metadata is cached for five seconds and invalidated on writes; _fetch_all_metadata paginates in 1000-row batches because ChromaDB silently truncates at 10K rows. Diary tools normalize agent names to lowercase for case-insensitive reads. An idle watchdog exits after MEMPALACE_MCP_IDLE_HOURS, default eight hours, to release ChromaDB file handles on Windows, and opt-in eager warmup pre-loads the embedder to avoid timeout errors on large palaces. Tool categories are Read seven, Write five, KG six, Tunnels six, Diaries two, and Settings three.

title: Hooks & Auto-save
summary: Two Claude Code hooks (Stop and PreCompact) auto-save session transcripts to the palace in the background without blocking the chat window, saving roughly USD 1 per session by writing diary entries via a direct Python API call instead of retyping them in chat.
body: MemPalace ships two Claude Code hooks, Stop and PreCompact, that auto-save session transcripts into the palace without interrupting the chat window. The Stop hook fires after each assistant response, counts human (non-command-message) entries in the session JSONL transcript, and triggers a checkpoint when the count since the last save reaches SAVE_INTERVAL (default 15, configurable). When the threshold is met it logs state, derives the project wing name from the transcript path, and spawns detached background mining subprocesses for the transcript in convos mode and an optional MEMPAL_DIR in projects mode. The PreCompact hook fires just before context compression; unlike Stop it does not count messages or gate on a threshold, instead running a synchronous blocking mine so the transcript is physically filed before the AI loses access to it, then returning empty JSON so compaction proceeds. The Stop hook optimizes latency (background work, under a 500ms budget) while PreCompact optimizes safety (synchronous save). Silent mode, the default since v3.3.0, saves the diary entry directly by calling tool_diary_write from the MCP server as a Python function, then returns only a systemMessage notification, eliminating token retransmission of diary blocks and saving about USD 1 per session. Legacy blocking mode instead returns decision block to ask the AI to save manually via MCP tools mempalace_diary_write and mempalace_add_drawer; the stop_hook_active flag prevents infinite loops. Hook-spawned miners claim atomic per-target PID slots in ~/.mempalace/hook_state/mine_pids using os.open with O_CREAT O_EXCL, hashing the mine command of directory, mode, and wing into a slot filename to prevent concurrent mines of the same source while allowing distinct targets to run in parallel; stale slots are reclaimed by PID liveness or age, default 2 hours via MEMPALACE_MINE_TIMEOUT_HOURS. Detached subprocesses use POSIX start_new_session or Windows DETACHED_PROCESS, CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP, and CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB flags so the hook can exit immediately. The palace-root kill-switch _palace_root_exists checks that ~/.mempalace is a directory; if the user removes it, all hooks short-circuit before any disk access. The hooks.auto_save config (default True) gates all hook functionality. Wing derivation reads cwd metadata first, then path decoding, then defaults to wing_sessions. On Windows, liveness uses ctypes GetExitCodeProcess rather than os.kill which would terminate the process. macOS bash 3.2 lacks mapfile, so the shell hook parses Python output with sed. A safe default selects silent mode when the config is unreadable. The hook harness timeout is 30 seconds while the mine subprocess can run 60 or more seconds independently in the background.

title: LLM Integration
summary: MemPalace layers optional, pluggable LLM assistance over five domains: entity refinement, closet regeneration, corpus-origin detection, room detection, and fact-checking. Every LLM step is opt-in and local-first, with external providers available only via explicit BYOK and always behind a privacy warning. When an LLM fails the system falls back to its heuristic/regex baseline transparently.
body: MemPalace provides optional, pluggable LLM assistance across five domains: entity refinement reclassifies regex-detected names into person/project/topic/common-word/ambiguous; closet regeneration extracts richer topics, quotes, and summaries from drawer content; corpus-origin detection decides whether content is AI-dialogue versus prose; room detection maps folder structure to a room map; and fact-checking compares text against the entity registry and knowledge graph. All LLM steps are opt-in and local-first by default. Three providers share a common interface: Ollama on localhost:11434 for full offline operation, OpenAI-compatible endpoints covering LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM, Groq, OpenRouter, and Together, and Anthropic for explicit bring-your-own-key use. External APIs are never enabled silently and always trigger a privacy warning before first use. The llm_client module defines an LLMProvider base class with three concrete implementations and a get_provider factory that forwards unknown kwargs like num_ctx to provider constructors. Privacy is enforced by _endpoint_is_local, a single source of truth that classifies localhost, RFC1918 private ranges, Tailscale CGNAT, mDNS .local hostnames, and IPv6 unique-local addresses as local; non-HTTP schemes such as file:// are rejected to prevent exfiltration. Entity refinement batches candidates twenty-five at a time with sampled context lines, skips authoritative git-backed entries, parses responses with a six-strategy JSON extraction fallback, and is Ctrl-C safe with partial results preserved. Closet regeneration uses any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, retries up to three times with exponential backoff on decode failure or HTTP 429/503, pages large palaces in batches of 5000 to dodge a SQLite variable-number crash, and leaves regex closets as the permanent fallback. Corpus-origin detection runs a fast Tier-1 heuristic always plus an optional Tier-2 LLM, merging only platform, user, and persona names without overwriting heuristic confidence. Fact-checking is purely offline, detecting similar-name typos via edit distance up to two, relationship mismatches, and stale facts, using an O(m times n) optimization rather than all-pairs comparison. Room detection infers structure from folder names and filenames with zero API calls. When an LLM is unavailable or fails, every pipeline falls back to its heuristic, regex, or offline-validation baseline and records what happened transparently, so no operation blocks and no data is silently discarded.

title: Internationalization
summary: MemPalace localizes UI and entity detection across 14 languages via JSON catalogs in mempalace/i18n/, with case-insensitive BCP 47 tags, script-aware word boundaries for combining marks, and optional multilingual embeddinggemma-300m embeddings.
body: MemPalace's internationalization layer localizes both UI strings and entity detection across 14 languages: en, ja, ko, zh-CN, zh-TW, de, es, fr, pt-br, it, ru, hi, id, and be. Each language is one JSON catalog under mempalace/i18n/ that serves two purposes at once: UI strings (terms, CLI messages, AAAK compression instruction) and entity-detection patterns (candidate patterns, person verb patterns, boundary characters). The loader, load_lang, reads a locale file after normalizing the requested BCP 47 tag through _canonical_lang, which lowercases and glob-matches so PT-BR, pt-br, and Pt-Br all resolve to the same on-disk file. The t function looks up dotted keys like cli.mine_complete, interpolates kwargs, and falls back to the key or English when a string is missing. A central problem this area solves is non-Latin script support. Python's built-in word boundary, backslash-b, is a transition between word characters and non-word characters, but Unicode combining marks such as Hindi matras and Arabic vowels are not word characters. As a result a literal boundary truncates names like अनीता to अनीत. The _script_boundary function builds a lookaround-based boundary that treats locale-declared boundary_chars as word-internal, preserving combining marks and multi-codepoint names. These boundaries are baked into patterns during collection rather than patched up afterward. get_entity_patterns merges patterns from multiple locales, deduplicating list fields while preserving order, unioning stopwords, and caching results by canonical language tuple so case variants share one cache entry. Only zh-CN, hi, and ko ship full entity sections; other locales reuse English entity detection. For semantic retrieval, the embedding subsystem offers two ChromaDB-compatible embedding functions. The default minilm (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) is English-only and faster. The optional EmbeddinggemmaONNX wraps a 300MB quantized embeddinggemma-300m model supporting 100+ languages, lazy-loaded from HuggingFace on first use, achieving 0.88 cross-lingual cosine similarity versus MiniLM's 0.35. It truncates its 768-dim output to 384-dim via Matryoshka Representation Learning so it drops into existing collections without schema migration, and L2-normalizes. Because ChromaDB persists the embedding function name on each collection, switching models requires a rebuild-index. Device resolution via _resolve_providers maps cpu, cuda, coreml, dml, and auto to ONNX Runtime providers with CPU fallback and one-shot warnings. The Dialect class loads locale-specific AAAK instructions and regex to guide lossy compression. Configuration reads entity_languages and embedding_model to select which languages apply and whether to use multilingual embeddings.

title: Security & Privacy
summary: MemPalace is privacy-by-architecture: all data lives locally with no external APIs for core operations and zero phone-home, reinforced by defense-in-depth input validation, prompt-contamination mitigation, MCP stdio protection, symlink-attack rejection, hardened hooks, and strict file permissions.
body: MemPalace is privacy by architecture. All user data, including drawers, the knowledge graph, embeddings, and indices, lives in ~/.mempalace/palace and never leaves the local machine. Core memory operations such as mining, searching, and embedding run locally by default and require no cloud account or internet connectivity. External providers like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Ollama are supported only through explicit user configuration via env vars or config.json and are never enabled silently. No telemetry library is imported, which eliminates the entire class of unintended exfiltration bugs because the code path simply does not exist. This architectural guarantee is reinforced by several hardening layers. Input validation runs at every boundary through sanitizers in config.py. The sanitize_name function blocks path traversal using checks for dot-dot, forward slash, and backslash, rejects null bytes and non-ASCII symbol characters, and enforces a 128 character limit. The sanitize_content function rejects null bytes and enforces a 100KB ceiling. The sanitize_kg_value function is more permissive, allowing punctuation, but still rejects null bytes and over-length strings. All sanitizers call strip_lone_surrogates to replace lone UTF-16 surrogates with U+FFFD before encoding, preventing ChromaDB encode crashes from issue 1235. Those lone surrogates come from MCP clients like Claude Desktop relaying corrupted clipboard data, not from user error. Prompt contamination mitigation lives in query_sanitizer.py. When AI agents prepend long system prompts to search queries, retrieval collapses from 89.8 percent to 1.0 percent. A four-stage pipeline of passthrough, question extraction, tail-sentence extraction, and tail truncation recovers intent, with worst-case recovery around 70 to 80 percent and common cases at 85 to 89 percent. The MCP server protects stdio by redirecting stdout to stderr at both the Python and file-descriptor level before heavy imports, so transitive libraries like onnxruntime or PostHog telemetry cannot corrupt JSON-RPC. The exporter rejects symlinks using O_NOFOLLOW on POSIX, which fails atomically with ELOOP and closes the TOCTOU window, falling back to an islink pre-check on Windows. Config files use 0o600 and directories use 0o700, applied atomically via umask or os.open flags. The save hook parses JSON with Python rather than shell eval, sanitizes session IDs to alphanumerics, validates transcript paths to .json or .jsonl suffixes with dot-dot rejection, and avoids mapfile for bash 3.2 compatibility on macOS. LLM endpoint configuration validates that the URL scheme is http or https only, rejecting file:// to prevent local-file exfiltration.

title: Repair, Sync & Maintenance
summary: Seven modules provide incremental-only Palace maintenance: repair, sync, migrate, export, dedup, spellcheck, and sweep. All operations are crash-safe and follow the never-destroy promise.
body: The MemPalace maintenance area is seven modules that keep a long-lived Palace consistent, deduplicated, and recoverable. Every operation obeys an incremental-only invariant: it appends new data or deletes explicitly-marked corrupt entries, but never overwrites existing correct rows, so a crash mid-operation leaves intact data untouched. repair.py offers four tiers: status (read-only health check comparing SQLite row count vs HNSW element count), scan (find unfetchable drawer IDs), prune (delete only corrupt IDs), and rebuild (extract all, back up only chroma.sqlite3, delete and recreate the collection, re-upsert). The extraction-cap guard from issue 1208 checks SQLite directly before any destructive operation; if SQLite reports more drawers than extraction yielded, rebuild aborts with recovery instructions rather than silently destroying data. The real case had 67,580 drawers on disk but only 10,000 returned through the ChromaDB API. Poisoned max_seq_id rows from a 0.6.x shim misfire are detected using a 2 to the 53rd power threshold, the float64 exact-integer ceiling, and un-poisoned non-destructively. Rebuilds use a two-phase live swap staging into a temp collection first and tracking a live_replaced flag for recovery. The FTS5 full-text index is atomically rebuilt and SQLite pages reclaimed via VACUUM. sync.py removes drawers whose source files are now gitignored, deleted, or out of scope, reusing the same GitignoreMatcher infrastructure as miner.py, holding the mine lock for the whole classify and apply window. Apply mode refuses to run without explicit wing or project_dirs scope. migrate.py rebuilds a Palace across ChromaDB versions, extracting directly from chroma.sqlite3 when the API fails, validating a write round-trip to catch silent-drop failures, then atomically swapping with an EXDEV copy-and-delete fallback and rollback guards. exporter.py streams drawers in paginated batches of 1000 to markdown organized by wing and room, with O_NOFOLLOW symlink defense closing the TOCTOU window. dedup.py groups drawers by source_file and consolidates near-identical drawers by cosine distance, greedily keeping the longest version. spellcheck.py corrects user messages while preserving technical terms, URLs, CamelCase, ALL_CAPS, words with digits, and known entity names. sweeper.py ingests Claude Code jsonl transcripts message-by-message using deterministic IDs like sweep_SESSION_UUID and per-session ISO-8601 cursors for idempotent, resume-safe reruns.

title: Benchmarks
summary: MemPalace's benchmark suite reports reproducible retrieval recall on three public datasets with an unusually transparent methodology, including disclosure of where it teaches to the test.
body: MemPalace's benchmarks measure retrieval recall@k on three public academic datasets and document an unusually honest methodology. The headline result is 96.6 percent recall at 5 on 500 LongMemEval questions using raw semantic search: each conversation session is stored as a single document of concatenated user turns, ChromaDB embeds documents and queries with the default all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence transformer at 384 dimensions, and the top five sessions are returned by cosine similarity. This baseline needs no heuristics, no LLM, and no API key, and reproduces on a laptop in five minutes. It contradicts the assumption that AI must extract and compress memory: verbatim storage avoids the information loss of extraction, and on ConvoMem it scores 92.9 percent average recall versus Mem0's 30 to 45 percent. A four-version hybrid re-ranker layers targeted fixes on top. Hybrid v1 adds keyword overlap scoring with a 0.30 weight that reduces distance by up to 30 percent. Hybrid v2 adds temporal date parsing and proximity boosting capped at 40 percent, plus two-pass assistant retrieval that finds a session with user turns then re-indexes with full text to avoid diluting the global index. Hybrid v3 adds 16 preference-extraction regex patterns that create synthetic documents sharing the session corpus_id, capped at 10 mentions. Hybrid v4 adds quoted-phrase and person-name boosting for the final three failures, which the authors flag as teaching to the test. A clean 50 development and 450 held-out train/test split yields 98.4 percent recall at 5 on unseen data as the honest publishable number, while 100 percent comes only from tuning on the test set itself. An optional LLM rerank sends the top ten sessions to Claude Haiku, which promotes one session to rank one, costing about 0.001 dollars per query and pushing results to at least 99 percent. Across datasets MemPalace scores 96.6 percent, 98.4 percent, and at least 99 percent on LongMemEval, 88.9 percent recall at 10 on LoCoMo, 92.9 percent average on ConvoMem, and 80.3 percent recall at 5 on MemBench. Every per-question result is committed as JSONL so readers can audit failures, and the three contaminated question ids d6233ab6, 4dfccbf8, and ceb54acb are named explicitly. Key functions live in benchmarks/longmemeval_bench.py, including build_palace_and_retrieve, the hybrid v1 through v4 variants, extract_keywords, keyword_overlap, extract_preferences, parse_time_offset_days, ndcg, and a module-level EphemeralClient singleton that broke a memory wall causing crashes at question 388.

title: Surprises & Gotchas
summary: The highest-signal cross-cutting page: curated insights, gotchas, performance notes, and security findings from across MemPalace, each traced to a line of code.
body: This page aggregates the most surprising, non-obvious, and watch-out findings across MemPalace, grouped into four kinds and each traceable to source. Key insights: raw verbatim text beats LLM-extracted memory by roughly 2x on LongMemEval (96.6% R@5 vs 30-45% for extraction systems like Mem0) because extraction discards context and loses the original when it fails. Closets are a ranking signal that only boosts, never a gate that filters, so weak closets can only help search. The corpus-origin pipeline treats the local LLM as a scalpel, discarding its verdict when it disagrees with a confident regex heuristic. BM25 IDF is computed over the candidate set rather than the corpus, which is correct for discriminating within results. Date-only knowledge-graph facts are normalized into full-day intervals at query time. The fact-checker uses two regexes rather than NLP to stay ultra-conservative, preferring false-negatives to false-positives. Gotchas: a per-thread re-entrant lock prevents the mine pipeline from deadlocking against itself; macOS bash 3.2 cannot use mapfile so the hook parses with sed; Windows cannot probe a PID with os.kill(pid,0) and uses GetExitCodeProcess; Python's word boundary truncates names with Unicode combining marks; switching embedding models silently breaks a palace via name mismatch, and legacy palaces silently default to L2 distance breaking cosine scores; KG predicates are lowercased and foreign keys are soft constraints; RTF bypasses MarkItDown for striprtf; init is made idempotent only by filtering its own artifacts. Performance: ChromaDB silently truncates at 10K rows so metadata is paginated; absolute cosine keeps ranking stable; the HNSW divergence floor scales with the sync threshold; emotion detection is keyword-based and zero-token; the Stop hook runs async while PreCompact runs sync. Security: MCP stdio is redirected at the file-descriptor level before heavy imports because C libraries write to fd 1; the pickle health check sniff-tests bytes without deserializing; non-HTTP LLM endpoints are rejected at parse time to block file exfiltration; the query sanitizer turns a silent recall cliff from system-prompt contamination into a graceful 70-89% degradation.
